cover.title: Rebuilding Lebanon’s Fiscal Contract for a Fairer Society
cover.hook: Lebanon’s 2027 draft budget balances at around $7 billion. **Who pays, and who benefits?**

chapters.title: A balanced budget. What does it tell us?

text: Start with the size of the state. In 2019, public expenditure stood at about **$15.2 billion**.
Then came the financial collapse. By 2026, spending had fallen to **$6 billion**.
The **2027 draft budget** would spend **around $7 billion**. Measured on the same scale, the state remains a fraction of what it was.
And on paper, it balances. Projected revenue: **around $7 billion**. Projected spending: **around $7 billion**. A projected deficit of zero.
But a zero deficit is not a clean slate. The state’s **debt and accumulated liabilities** remain unaddressed.
Nor does the balance say anything about who finances the state, or who benefits from it.

chapters.teaser: On paper, the books close. That is where the questions begin.

chapters.title: Who pays?

text: Compare two groups of Lebanese households.
The **poorest half** earn income equal to 11% of GDP. In 2019, they paid **20%** of all taxes. By 2026, they paid **26%**.
At the other end, the **richest 1%** earn income equal to 20% of GDP and hold about one-third of national wealth.
Over the same years, their share of all taxes fell from **14% to 7%**.
Look at what Lebanon taxes. **About 79%** of tax revenue comes from **consumption taxes**, collected on what households buy.
Income, profits and wealth remain largely untaxed.
The 2027 draft continues this pattern. It projects **total revenue rising by 14.2%**.
Where would the new money come from? **Fuel taxes and VAT** account for **more than half** of the additional tax revenue.
Exemptions stay in place without justification, and revenue targets rest on optimistic assumptions amid a contracting economy.

chapters.teaser: The tax burden has shifted toward the households with the least.

chapters.title: Who benefits from public spending?

text: Now follow the money out.
Public spending that can be traced to the people it benefits fell from **$13 billion in 2019** to **$4.3 billion in 2026**.
For the **poorest half of households**, the amount fell from **$814 million** to **$617 million**.
What still reached them came mostly through public hospitalization and social protection.
And for every $100 of traceable spending in 2026, **youth and families received $15**.

chapters.teaser: Less spending reaches people, and less of it reaches the poorest.

chapters.title: Where does the proposed spending increase go?

text: The 2027 draft raises spending. **More than 90%** of that increase goes to **personnel costs**.
That would make personnel costs **65% of the entire budget**.
Capital spending, meanwhile, would rise by **only around $25 million**, in a country with vast reconstruction and infrastructure needs.
Resources that reach people directly remain limited.

chapters.teaser: The 2027 draft spends more. Almost all of the increase goes to one line.

questions.title: What should Lebanon’s budget do over the next five years?
questions.intro: Over the next five years, Lebanon’s budget will have to answer four.
items: How should Lebanon raise and allocate public resources?
What reforms would make those choices possible?
questions.teaser: A budget can balance and still leave the hardest questions unanswered.

purpose.title: From shortcomings to a roadmap
purpose.intro: TPI’s roundtable brings policymakers, public officials and experts together to move the debate from what the budget gets wrong to what it should become.

items.title: A shared starting point
items.text: Participants will use TPI’s research on who pays taxes and who benefits from public spending as a common evidence base.

items.title: Concrete options
items.text: They will debate options for taxation, exemptions, spending and public financial management.

items.title: Feasibility and trade-offs
items.text: They will examine the feasibility and trade-offs of reforms, including their effects on vulnerable households.

prologue.label: Prologue
lines: Every budget is a contract between a state and its people.
It decides **who pays** for the state, and **who the state serves**.
Lebanon’s 2027 draft budget, now before Parliament, balances on paper at **around $7 billion**.
A balance answers one question. This story follows the two it leaves open.

closing.title: What should the budget be?
closing.text: Areas of agreement and open questions from the roundtable will inform TPI’s forthcoming report of the same name.
